name: Watt six-bar linkage
summary: Two four-bar loops sharing a ternary rocker: a turning crank drives a first rocker, which drives a second rocker with a reshaped swing.

ratio.typical: output swing set by the second loop, about 90° here for 360° of crank

topology.notes: Watt topology: the two ternary links (ground and the middle rocker) share joint O4; two four-bar loops

explain.motion: A crank-rocker loop O2-A-B-O4 turns the crank's rotation into a rocking of the middle link. That middle rocker is a triangle: its second arm O4-C drives a second loop C-D-O6, so the output rocker at O6 swings by an amount and with a timing that the second loop reshapes.
explain.forces: Torque passes from the crank through two pin-ended couplers in series, so each coupler only pushes or pulls. Transmission angles in both loops must stay roughly between 40° and 140°; near a toggle in either loop the output force grows while the motion stalls.
explain.benefits: It gives more design freedom than a four-bar (amplified swing, dwell, better timing) while still using only pin joints.
explain.limits: Errors and clearances in two loops add up, and a poor second loop can lock or flip branch. Synthesis is harder than for a single four-bar.

build.ground: frame holding O2 (0,0), O4 (100,0) and O6 (180,60)

members.def: ternary plate pivoted at O4: O4→B 60 and O4→C 50, arm O4C set 90° clockwise from O4B

build.defining_relations: Loop 1 Grashof: s+l <= p+q, 30+100 <= 60+100, so the crank turns fully. Loop 2 is a closure C(theta4) to O6 with |CD| = e, |O6D| = f. Mobility 3(6-1)-2*7 = 1.
build.range: crank 360° continuous; rocker1 swings 62° (74° to 136°); rocker2 swings about 91° (116° to 208°); transmission angle in loop 2 stays 56° to 123°
build.plot: rocker1 and rocker2 angle vs crank angle
build.notes: Solve loop 1 with B on the upper branch (circleX(A,b,O4,c,+1) in site convention), then C = O4 + 50 at angle(O4B) - 90°, then D = circleX(C,60,O6,30,+1). Keep the same branch all cycle. This is the Watt II arrangement (two four-bars in series); Watt I grounds a binary link instead.

examples.detail: Watt's straight-line beam linkage with its copying links forms a Watt-type chain, as listed under six-bar applications.

name: Stephenson six-bar linkage
summary: A four-bar whose coupler point drives an extra two-link dyad, so the output follows the coupler curve and can dwell or swing widely.

ratio.typical: about 54° of output swing per crank turn here

topology.notes: Stephenson topology: ternary ground and ternary coupler separated by binary links; one four-bar loop and one five-bar loop

explain.motion: A crank-rocker four-bar O2-A-B-O4 has a triangular coupler; a point P on it traces a closed coupler curve. A link P-D ties that point to an output rocker O6-D, so the rocker follows the curve. Where the curve runs along an arc centred on D, the output pauses.
explain.forces: Crank torque passes through the ternary coupler and the dyad link, each pin-ended bar carrying push or pull. The output rocker sees high force but little motion near its toggle positions.
explain.benefits: It can give dwells, large swings or special timing with only pin joints and one input.
explain.limits: Coupler curves are sensitive to dimensions and wear, and branch flips are possible if the dyad nears a straight line. Design needs simulation or synthesis software.

members.def: ternary plate: A→B 60, coupler point P at local (30,-40) from A with x along AB

build.defining_relations: Four-bar Grashof: 20+60 <= 50+60, crank fully rotates. Output closure |P(theta)D| = e, |O6D| = f. Mobility 3(6-1)-2*7 = 1. Stephenson I, II, III differ by which link is ground; this is III (dyad from coupler to ground).
build.range: crank 360° continuous; coupler point P sweeps a 42 x 19 mm loop; rocker2 swings about 54° (-49° to 5°)
build.plot: rocker2 angle vs crank angle, with the coupler curve of P
build.notes: B = circleX(A,60,O4,50,+1); D = circleX(P,70,O6,40,+1). Show P's coupler curve as a path; the dyad PD and rocker2 must not pass straight or the branch flips.

name: Five-bar linkage
summary: A closed loop of five bars with two driven cranks, so one end point can be steered anywhere in a planar workspace.

ratio.typical: 2 inputs map to an x-y point; scale set by arm lengths

topology.notes: two grounded motors; a gear pair between the cranks makes it a 1-DOF geared five-bar

explain.motion: Two cranks turn about fixed pivots O1 and O2. Each carries a distal bar, and the two distal bars meet at the tip P. Setting both crank angles fixes P, so moving them together steers P along any path in the workspace.
explain.forces: Both motors sit on the base, so the moving parts are light and forces at P are shared by two arms. Near singular poses (distal bars in line, or a crank in line with its distal bar) stiffness or control is lost.
explain.benefits: Low moving inertia, high stiffness and easy backdriving make it good for fast pick-and-place, plotters and haptic devices.
explain.limits: The workspace is smaller than a serial arm's and is bounded by singularities. Two motors and inverse kinematics are needed.

build.input: crankL and crankR, each driven by its own motor (demo: thetaL = 120° + 30° sin u, thetaR = 60° + 30° sin(u + 90°))
build.defining_relations: Forward kinematics: P = circleX(A, l2, B, l2, +1) with A = O1 + l1(cos thetaL, sin thetaL), B = O2 + l1(cos thetaR, sin thetaR). Inverse: each crank angle from the triangle O-joint-P with sides l1, l2, |OP|. Mobility 3(5-1)-2*5 = 2.
build.range: each crank ±30° about its demo centre; tip P moves over a 62 x 59 mm loop (x -6 to 56, y 73 to 132)
build.plot: tip x and y vs phase u
build.notes: Use the elbows-out, tip-up branch (side +1). Two independent inputs; for a 1-DOF demo couple them with a fixed phase or a 1:1 gear. Avoid poses where A, P, B line up.

name: Klann linkage
summary: Joe Klann's six-bar walking leg: one crank moves a foot along a flat stance stroke and then lifts it high for the return step.

ratio.typical: foot stride about 3.8 x crank radius, lift about 2 x crank radius

topology.notes: modified Stephenson III chain; ternary connecting member and ternary leg

explain.motion: The crank turns the connecting member, whose middle pin E is held by a short lower rocker, so its far end K swings in a loop. The leg is a rigid bar pinned at the hip H to an upper rocker and at the knee K to the connecting member. The foot at its tip moves along a nearly flat line for about a third of the turn and then lifts and swings back.
explain.forces: Ground reaction at the foot travels up the leg into the two rockers and the crank, so the long leg bar sees bending. Two legs half a cycle apart on one crank share the load and keep the frame level.
explain.benefits: High foot lift lets it step over obstacles and climb stairs, using only pin joints and one rotary drive per side.
explain.limits: The stance is not perfectly flat or constant speed, and the foot path is fixed by the geometry. The long leg bar must be stiff; joint play shows up as foot wobble.

build.ground: frame with crank axis O (0,0), upper rocker pivot A (-17.4,46.0) and lower rocker pivot B (-44.0,-13.1)
build.output: foot point F on the leg, path traced

members.def: rigid triangle C, E, K: CE 44.0, EK 39.0, CK 82.5 (K at local (82.0,-8.7) in frame C→E)
rigid triangle H, K, F: HK 66.9, KF 66.9, HF 129.3 (F at local (124.9,33.5) in frame H→K)

build.defining_relations: Dimensions scaled (x74.63) from the pivot coordinates in US patent 6,260,862 so that the crank is 20 mm. Mobility 3(6-1)-2*7 = 1. Foot path approx. 75 mm wide x 39 mm high at a 20 mm crank.
build.range: crank 360° continuous; foot F sweeps x -119 to -44, y -60 to -20 (75 x 39 mm); flat stance over roughly a third of the turn
build.notes: Crank angle 0 = C at (-20,0) (pointing toward the leg). E = circleX(C,44.0,B,23.9,-1); K from the connector frame; H = circleX(K,66.9,A,38.6,+1); F from the leg frame. These branches reproduce the patent pose at angle 0. For a walker, pair a mirror leg 180° out of phase.

name: Jansen's linkage
summary: Theo Jansen's Strandbeest leg: one crank and eleven bars move the foot along a long flat stride and lift it on the way back.

ratio.typical: flat stride about 4 x crank radius (124 mm at a 30 mm crank), lift about 45 mm

topology.notes: ground, crank, bars j, k, c, f, upper triangle and foot triangle; joints at A, Y and C each join three bodies

explain.motion: The crank turns about O. Bars j and k carry its motion to the upper triangle (pivoted at the fixed point Y) and to bar c, and the two rigid triangles pass it down to the foot. For about half the turn the foot slides along a nearly flat line, then it lifts and swings forward to start the next step.
explain.forces: During the stride the ground pushes up on the foot; the load travels through the foot triangle and bars into the fixed pivot Y and the crank. Every bar other than the two triangles is pinned at both ends, so it only pushes or pulls. Because the foot stays level, the crank does little lifting work during the stride.
explain.benefits: All joints are plain pins and the leg has one degree of freedom, so one shaft drives many legs. The flat stride keeps the body at a steady height.
explain.limits: Eleven bars and many pins add friction and play, and the foot path is fixed by the holy numbers. It walks well only on fairly flat ground and is slow to climb.

build.ground: frame holding crank axis O (0,0) and pivot Y (-76,-15.6)
build.output: foot point F on the foot triangle, path traced

members.def: rigid triangle Y, B, D: YB b 83, BD e 111.6, YD d 80.2
rigid triangle C, E, F: CE g 73.4, EF h 131.4, CF i 98

build.defining_relations: Jansen's holy numbers a 38, b 41.5, c 39.3, d 40.1, e 55.8, f 39.4, g 36.7, h 65.7, i 49, j 50, k 61.9, l 7.8, m 15 (site scales by 2). Mobility 3(8-1)-2*10 = 1.
build.range: crank 360° continuous; foot F spans x -143 to -7 and y -184 to -139 (136 x 45 mm); flat stance (within 3 mm of the lowest point) for about 48% of the turn over 124 mm
build.plot: foot height above its lowest point vs crank angle
build.notes: Site solve: A = O + m(cos u, sin u); B = circleX(A,j,Y,b,-1); C = circleX(A,k,Y,c,+1); D = circleX(B,e,Y,d,-1); E = circleX(D,f,C,g,-1); F = circleX(E,h,C,i,-1). Built in three 5 mm planes; triangles as plate pairs straddling the bars. A full walker mirrors the leg about the crank and phases several legs on one crankshaft.

name: Ackermann steering linkage
summary: A trapezoid of axle, steering arms and tie rod that turns the inner front wheel more than the outer so both roll round one centre.

ratio.typical: outer angle about 0.83 x inner angle at 30° (24.9° vs 30°)

topology.notes: four-bar: axle beam (ground), left knuckle arm, tie rod, right knuckle arm; real cars add a rack or drag link to drive it

explain.motion: Each front wheel steers about its kingpin on a knuckle with a steering arm. The arms point inward toward the centre of the rear axle and are joined by a tie rod, forming a trapezoid. When one wheel steers, the tie rod turns the other wheel by a smaller angle on the outside of the turn.
explain.forces: Steering force enters one knuckle and crosses to the other through the tie rod in push or pull. Tyre side forces feed back through the same path, so the linkage is fully backdrivable.
explain.benefits: Wheels roll on concentric circles at low speed, cutting tyre scrub and wear and making tight turns smooth.
explain.limits: A four-bar only approximates the ideal relation, best near one design angle. At high speed tyre slip angles matter more, so race cars often use parallel or reverse Ackermann.

build.ground: front axle beam with kingpins KL (-75,0) and KR (75,0); rear axle centre at (0,-250)
build.input: left knuckle arm, rocked ±40° about KL
build.output: right knuckle angle about KR (outer or inner wheel)

members.def: knuckle + steering arm at KL, arm 30 pointing toward the rear axle centre (16.7° inward of straight back)
knuckle + steering arm at KR, arm 30, mirror of armL

build.defining_relations: Ideal Ackermann: cot(delta_outer) - cot(delta_inner) = w / L. Arms point at the rear axle centre: beta = atan((w/2)/L). Tie rod t = w - 2 r sin(beta).
build.plot: outer wheel angle vs inner wheel angle, with the ideal Ackermann curve
build.notes: Tie rod behind the axle. PR = circleX(PL, t, KR, r, -1) (pick the branch with PR behind the axle). Draw wheel axis lines meeting near the rear-axle line to show the turning centre.

examples.detail: Road vehicles use Ackermann-type tie rod or rack geometry, often partly Ackermann.

name: Rhombic drive
summary: Two geared counter-rotating cranks and a jointed rhombus drive two coaxial pistons with a phase lag and no side thrust.

ratio.typical: each piston stroke about 2.4 x crank radius here (47.7 mm at r = 20)

topology.notes: ground, two crank gears, four equal rods, power piston and displacer; the count is over-constrained and moves thanks to symmetry, the gear mesh keeps the cranks mirrored

explain.motion: Two equal gears mesh and turn in opposite directions, each with a crank pin. Four equal rods join the two pins to an upper yoke on the power piston and a lower yoke on the displacer, forming a rhombus. As the cranks turn, the rhombus flattens and stretches, and the two pistons slide along the same axis with a phase lag of about 70° to 90°.
explain.forces: Gas force on each piston splits equally into two rods, and the sideways components cancel, so the pistons need almost no side guidance. The gears carry the torque difference between the two cranks.
explain.benefits: Perfect dynamic balance with no side thrust on the seals lets beta Stirling engines run smooth, quiet and pressurised.
explain.limits: Many precise parts, close tolerances and a gear pair make it costly. Wear in the gears lets the cranks drift from mirror symmetry.

build.ground: crankcase with gear centres G1 (-30,0) and G2 (30,0) and the cylinder axis x = 0
build.input: gas force on the power piston (demo: drive gear1 at constant speed)
build.output: gear angle and the two piston positions on the y axis

members.def: centre G1 (-30,0), pitch radius 30, crank pin PL at 20 from centre
centre G2 (30,0), pitch radius 30, crank pin PR at 20, mirror of gear1
power piston yoke T on the y axis, above
displacer yoke Bt on the y axis, below

params.name: e
params.note: gear centre offset from the axis

params.name: z
params.note: teeth per gear, module 2, centres 60 apart

build.defining_relations: PR = (e + r cos t, r sin t), PL = (-e - r cos t, r sin t). y_piston = r sin t + sqrt(L^2 - (e + r cos t)^2); y_displacer = r sin t - sqrt(L^2 - (e + r cos t)^2). Gears 1:1 counter-rotating.
build.range: gears 360° continuous; piston y 26.5 to 74.2 (stroke 47.7); displacer y -74.2 to -26.5 (stroke 47.7); displacer leads piston by about 70°; yokes never closer than 66 mm
build.plot: piston and displacer positions vs crank angle
build.notes: Gears turn opposite ways; set gear2 angle = pi - gear1 angle so the pins stay mirrored. In a real engine the displacer rod passes through a hollow piston rod; draw them coaxial.

examples.detail: Philips developed the rhombic drive for its MP1002CA generator set and later Stirling engines.
The Lanchester twin-cylinder car engine around 1900 used a rhombic drive to balance its pistons.

name: Watt's linkage
summary: Two equal rockers joined by a short bar: the bar's midpoint moves on a nearly straight line, drawing a figure eight at the extremes.

ratio.typical: about 74 mm of near-straight travel for ±24° of rocker swing at r = 90

topology.notes: crossed double-rocker four-bar; tracer at coupler midpoint

explain.motion: Two equal rockers pivot on opposite sides, one high and one low, and a short coupler joins their tips. As the rockers swing, each tip moves on an arc, and the arcs bend opposite ways, so the coupler midpoint moves almost straight. Over the full swing the midpoint draws a figure eight.
explain.forces: Each rocker is pinned at both ends, so it only pushes or pulls along its length. Loads across the line of motion are carried, which is why it locates an axle sideways.
explain.benefits: Three moving pin-jointed parts give good straight motion without sliders, and it is symmetric left to right.
explain.limits: Straightness holds only near the middle of the swing; deviation grows quickly toward the toggles. It needs room for two long rockers.

members.def: A→B, c = 60, tracer M at its midpoint

build.defining_relations: Equal rockers r, coupler c, pivots offset by c vertically and 2r horizontally so both rockers are horizontal when the coupler is vertical. Midpoint path is a Watt's curve (a lemniscate-like figure eight).
build.range: rockerL ±24°; midpoint M travels y -36 to +38 (74 mm) with x deviation under 0.6 mm; full figure eight when swung to the toggles where |A O2| = r + c
build.plot: midpoint offset from the ideal line vs input angle
build.notes: Site solve: A = O1 + r(cos th, sin th); B = circleX(A,c,O2,r,-1); M = midpoint. The ghost tracer G draws the whole figure eight by swinging to the toggles and switching branch there.

examples.detail: A Watt's link centres a live rear axle sideways, replacing a Panhard rod, as in the Opel Astra J and Mustang upgrades.
James Watt used it in 1784 to guide the piston rod of his double-acting beam engine.
Watt-type links guide axles and bogies laterally.

name: Chebyshev linkage
summary: Crossed rockers in the ratio 4:5:2 make the coupler midpoint run very nearly straight between the two pivots' verticals.

ratio.typical: stroke = ground length (120 mm here) for 53° of rocker swing

topology.notes: crossed double-rocker four-bar; tracer at coupler midpoint

explain.motion: Two long rockers pivot on a common base and cross each other; a short coupler joins their tips. When the left rocker swings from about 37° to 90°, the coupler midpoint moves from directly above one pivot to directly above the other along a nearly flat line.
explain.forces: The rockers are two-force members carrying push or pull. Near the ends of the stroke the transmission angle falls and the input torque needed rises.
explain.benefits: Very good straightness (0.3 mm over 120 mm here) from three moving pin-jointed parts.
explain.limits: Only a limited swing is straight, and the crossed rockers must sit in different planes so they can pass each other.

build.input: rockerL oscillating from 36.9° to 90° about O1
build.output: coupler midpoint M on the line y = 120

members.def: A→B, c = 2s = 60, tracer M at midpoint

build.defining_relations: Ratios ground : rocker : coupler = 4 : 5 : 2. Midpoint lies on y = d at both ends and the middle of the stroke. Input limits: acos(d/r) = 36.9° to 90°.
build.range: rockerL 36.9° to 90° (53°); midpoint M runs x 0 to 120 at y = 120 with deviation up to 0.29 mm
build.plot: midpoint offset from the ideal line vs input angle
build.notes: Site solve: B = O1 + r(cos th, sin th); A = circleX(B,c,O2,r,-1); M = midpoint. Rockers on layers 0 and 2 with the coupler between, because at the stroke ends one tip pin lies on the other rocker.

name: Hoekens linkage
summary: A crank-rocker whose extended coupler tip runs along a straight line at nearly constant speed for half of every crank turn.

ratio.typical: straight stroke = 4 x crank (160 mm at a 40 mm crank) per half turn

topology.notes: crank-rocker four-bar with the coupler extended past the rocker pin

explain.motion: A short crank turns fully about O2 and a rocker of 2.5 crank lengths swings about O4. The coupler is pinned to both and extends to a tip twice the rocker-pin distance from the crank pin. For half the crank turn the tip moves along a straight line at almost constant speed, then it returns along a raised arc.
explain.forces: The rocker is a two-force member. The long coupler overhang sees bending from any load at the tip, and the transmission angle at B should be watched near the return.
explain.benefits: Continuous crank input with a long, steady-speed straight stroke makes it a good walking leg or film-advance claw.
explain.limits: The return arc needs clearance, and straightness and speed are only approximate. The overhung tip amplifies joint play.

build.output: coupler tip T, straight line y = 160 for crank 90° to 270°

members.def: A→B 100, extended along AB to tip T at 200 from A

build.defining_relations: Ratios crank : ground : coupler : rocker = 1 : 2 : 2.5 : 2.5, tip at 5 crank lengths from A along AB. Grashof 1+2.5 <= 2+2.5, crank rotates fully. Cognate of the Chebyshev linkage.
build.range: crank 360° continuous; tip T on the line y = 160 from x 0 to 160 for crank 90° to 270° (deviation under 0.4 mm); return arc rises to y = 196; T spans x -14 to 174
build.plot: tip speed as % of its mean on the line vs crank angle
build.notes: Site solve: A = O2 + a(cos u, sin u); B = circleX(A,b,O4,c,+1); T = A + e(unit AB). Mean straight-line speed 4s per half turn.

name: Roberts linkage
summary: Equal rockers carrying an isosceles triangle: the triangle's apex moves almost straight along the line through the two pivots.

ratio.typical: about 80 mm of near-straight travel for 34° of rocker swing (ground 100)

topology.notes: symmetric double-rocker four-bar; tracer at the apex of the triangular coupler

explain.motion: Two equal rockers stand on pivots a distance 2b apart. Their tips carry the base of a triangular coupler whose two equal sides hang down to an apex P. As the rockers lean, P slides along the ground line between the pivots, almost straight.
explain.forces: The rockers carry push or pull only; loads at P bend the coupler plate. Straightness and stiffness fall near the stroke ends where the rockers get steep.
explain.benefits: Symmetric, compact and all pin-jointed, with the straight path lying conveniently on the line of the fixed pivots.
explain.limits: Straightness is approximate and the usable stroke is shorter than the pivot spacing. The apex passes between the pivots, which constrains the frame layout.

build.output: apex P of the coupler on the line y = 0

members.def: isosceles triangle: base B1C1 b = 50, sides B1P = C1P = a = 70, apex P on the ground side

build.defining_relations: Ground 2b, rockers a, coupler triangle sides a, a, b, apex P. At mid-stroke P lies on the pivot line; longer a (relative to b) gives straighter motion over a smaller fraction of the gap.
build.range: rockerL 50° to 84°; apex P travels x -40 to +40 along y = 0 with deviation under 0.4 mm
build.plot: apex offset from the pivot line vs input angle
build.notes: C1 = circleX(B1, b, O2, a, +1) (rockers leaning the same way, uncrossed). P = midpoint(B1C1) + h * unit normal pointing toward the ground line, h = sqrt(a^2 - b^2/4).

name: Evans grasshopper linkage
summary: A Scott Russell linkage with the slider replaced by a long swinging link: the beam end moves nearly straight with only pin joints.

ratio.typical: about 50 mm of near-straight travel for a 40° swing of the radius link (a = 50)

topology.notes: four-bar: radius link, beam and long swing link; tracer at the free end of the beam

explain.motion: A radius link of length a pivots at O1 and holds the middle of a beam of length 2a. One beam end B is held by a long swing link instead of a slider, so B moves on a gentle arc that is close to a straight line. The other end P then moves nearly straight along a line through O1, at right angles to B's path.
explain.forces: Load at P is shared by the radius link at mid-beam and the swing link at B; all three are pin-ended. The beam bends between its pins, and the swing link carries little load.
explain.benefits: Gives Scott Russell type straight motion without any sliding guide, so it lasts with little lubrication.
explain.limits: Straightness depends on the swing link being long, which makes the frame large. Deviation grows quickly outside the design stroke.

build.input: radius link oscillating 25° to 65° about O1
build.output: beam end P moving along the x axis

members.def: B→P, 2a = 100, pinned at its midpoint M

params.name: O2
params.note: swing link pivot, set at the middle of B's travel

build.defining_relations: Scott Russell core: |O1M| = |MB| = |MP| = a, so with B on the y axis P runs exactly on the x axis. The swing link of length b replaces the slider, giving an error of order (B travel)^2/(8b).
build.range: radius link 25° to 65°; P moves x 40 to 90 (50 mm) with deviation under 1.4 mm from y = 0; B moves about y 44 to 92 near x = 0
build.plot: beam end offset from the ideal line vs input angle
build.notes: B = the intersection of circle(M, a) and circle(O2, b) nearest to x = 0. P = 2M - B. In grasshopper engines the beam end drives the crank or is driven by the piston rod.

examples.detail: Half-beam engines guided the piston rod or crankpin with grasshopper linkages.
The PS Comet of 1812 used a grasshopper marine engine, a pattern that lasted about half a century.
Grasshopper locomotives of the Baltimore and Ohio railroad used the arrangement.

name: Scott Russell linkage
summary: A beam pinned at its midpoint to a crank of half its length: sliding one end along a line moves the other exactly at right angles.

ratio.typical: output y = 2a sin(phi), input x = 2a cos(phi); 1:1 at 45°

topology.notes: ground, crank, beam, slider; exact straight line for the beam end

explain.motion: A crank of length a pivots at O and holds the middle M of a beam of length 2a. One end B slides along the x axis. Because O, B and P all lie on a circle centred at M of radius a, the other end P moves exactly along the y axis through O.
explain.forces: The slider guide takes side load, which rises steeply as B approaches O and the crank lines up with the beam. The crank pin at M carries the main load in push or pull.
explain.benefits: An exact straight line at right angles to the input from only one slide and three pins, more compact than a Watt's linkage.
explain.limits: It needs a sliding or rolling guide for B, and it cannot pass through the position where B reaches O. Lateral force on the slider grows near that end.

build.ground: pivot O (0,0) and a slide along the x axis
build.input: slider B, linear along the x axis from x 95 to 20
build.output: beam end P, straight line along the y axis

members.def: pivot O (0,0) and guide on y = 0
block at B on the x axis

build.defining_relations: |OM| = |MB| = |MP| = a. With M = a(cos phi, sin phi): B = (2a cos phi, 0), P = (0, 2a sin phi). x_B^2 + y_P^2 = (2a)^2.
build.range: slider x 95 to 20 (phi 18° to 78°); P moves y 31 to 98 along x = 0 exactly
build.notes: Keep phi between about 10° and 80°; at phi = 90° B reaches O and the beam and crank turn together (singular). Other beam points trace ellipses, as in the elliptic trammel.

examples.detail: Some front-drive cars locate a solid rear axle with a Scott Russell type link using an elastomer joint in place of the slide.
Watchmaker William Freemantle patented it in Britain (patent 2741) for straight motion.
Used inside larger linkages and instruments to turn a slide into motion at right angles.

name: Peaucellier-Lipkin linkage
summary: An eight-bar inversor: as the input point moves on a circle through the fixed pivot, the output point moves on an exactly straight line.

ratio.typical: 175 mm of exact straight travel for ±64° of input swing

topology.notes: ground, input arm, two long arms, four rhombus sides; joints at O, A, B and C each join three bodies

explain.motion: Two long arms from the fixed pivot O hold opposite corners A and B of a rhombus whose other corners are C and D. O, C and D stay in line and OC x OD stays constant, so D is the inverse of C. A short input arm pivoted at Q makes C move on a circle through O, and the inverse of such a circle is a straight line, which D traces exactly.
explain.forces: All bars are pin-ended and carry only push or pull. Force at D reaches the input through the rhombus and long arms; mechanical advantage falls as C approaches O and D runs far out.
explain.benefits: It was the first planar linkage to give an exact straight line using only pin joints, with no slide.
explain.limits: Eight links and ten pins add play, and the arms must cross in several planes. Straight travel is limited by the arms reaching full stretch.

build.output: rhombus corner D moving along x = 140
build.defining_relations: OC x OD = l^2 - q^2 = 12600 mm^2. C on a circle of radius r through O gives D on the line x = (l^2 - q^2)/(2r) = 140.
build.range: input ±64°; D moves y -87.5 to +87.5 (175 mm) on x = 140 exactly
build.plot: D position along the line vs input angle
build.notes: Site solve: C = Q + r(cos phi, sin phi); A = circleX(O,l,C,q,+1); B = circleX(O,l,C,q,-1); D = A + B - C. Built on four planes 1.5 mm apart so links never collide. At phi near ±180° C reaches O and D runs to infinity.

examples.use: Steam engine and blowing engine guides
examples.detail: Exact pin-jointed guides were proposed and built to guide piston rods without a crosshead slide.
Reuleaux and Matemateca collections hold Peaucellier models to teach inversion.
Inversors were built as instruments to draw exact lines and circles.

name: Hart's inversor
summary: A six-bar inversor built on a crossed antiparallelogram: a point on a circle through the fixed pivot drives another along an exact line.

ratio.typical: about 113 mm of exact straight travel for ±80° of crank swing

topology.notes: ground, crank, and the four bars of an antiparallelogram (one short bar pivoted to ground at its midpoint)

explain.motion: Four bars form a crossed antiparallelogram: two long bars CD and EF and two short bars CE and FD. The midpoints of all four bars always lie on one line, and the product of distances from one midpoint to two others stays constant. With the midpoint A of CE fixed and the midpoint g of EF driven on a circle through A, the midpoint p of CD runs on an exact straight line.
explain.forces: All bars are pin-ended; the long bars also carry the mid-span pins g and p, so they see some bending. Near the ends of travel the crossed bars line up and force transmission drops.
explain.benefits: An exact straight line with six links instead of Peaucellier's eight.
explain.limits: The crank can only swing, not rotate, and the crossed bars must sit in different planes. Pins at mid-bar need stiff bars.

build.input: crank oscillating ±80° about B (from the position pointing away from A)
build.output: point p, midpoint of CD, on the line x = 67.5

members.def: B→g, 20, so g moves on a circle through A
short bar 60, pivoted to ground at its midpoint A
long bar 120, tracer p at its midpoint
long bar 120, crank pin g at its midpoint

build.defining_relations: Midpoints of the four bars are collinear; A p x A g = (l^2 - s^2)/4 = 2700 mm^2. With |AB| = |Bg| = 20, g lies on a circle through A, so p lies on the line x = 2700 / (2 x 20) = 67.5. Wikipedia example ratios AB = Bg = 2, CE = FD = 6, CD = EF = 12 (scaled x10).
build.range: crank ±80° about the far position (limit ±82.8° where |Ag| = 30); p moves y -56.6 to +56.6 (113 mm) on x = 67.5 exactly
build.plot: p position along the line vs crank angle
build.notes: Solve numerically: given g, find the angle alpha of CE about A so that |E g| = 60 (two roots; keep the root that keeps p, A, g collinear and continue it smoothly through 0°), then F = 2g - E, D = circleX(C,120,F,60) on the branch with |DF| = 60 and the bars crossed, p = midpoint of CD. Put the long bars in separate planes.

examples.detail: Schilling's series of kinematic models included a Hart inversor, now at the Smithsonian.
Proposed as a simpler exact guide than the Peaucellier cell for engines and instruments.
Used to demonstrate inversion and draw lines and circles exactly.
